text: Coral Triangle reef calcification rates of 1–10 kg CaCO₃/m²/year under historical conditions maintained reef structure against physical erosion; projections of ocean acidification under RCP8.5 suggest net reef erosion (calcification < dissolution) across most tropical reefs by 2050–2100, marking a fundamental transition in reef ecosystem function from carbonate accretion to erosion; even under optimistic emissions scenarios (RCP2.6), 90% of reefs would experience marginal calcification conditions, meaning the structural habitat supporting 25% of marine species would physically degrade over decades even if bleaching is reduced.

Sea level rise is not globally uniform: gravitational effects of melting ice sheets cause local sea level to fall near the melting ice while rising far away; if the West Antarctic Ice Sheet collapses, gravitational attraction reduction would lower sea level within 2,000 km of Antarctica while causing above-average rise in the North Atlantic, including the U.S. East Coast, London, and Tokyo; additionally, glacial isostatic adjustment (land rising as ancient ice age glaciers continue to unload) causes relative sea level to fall in Scandinavia and Scotland while rising in the U.S. mid-Atlantic, where land subsidence compounds the threat.

Phytoplankton consume dissolved CO₂ during photosynthesis, drawing down surface ocean pCO₂ to levels below the atmosphere during productive seasons and allowing atmospheric CO₂ to invade the surface ocean; in oligotrophic subtropical gyres, nutrient limitation keeps primary production low, and these regions are actually sources of CO₂ to the atmosphere in summer when warming reduces CO₂ solubility; satellite chlorophyll sensors estimate that ocean primary production totals approximately 50 Gt C/year—comparable to terrestrial primary production—of which less than 0.5 Gt C reaches the deep ocean via the biological pump in its most refractory form.

Marine Archaea—particularly Marine Group I Thaumarchaeota—carry out ammonia oxidation (nitrification) in the dark ocean, converting ammonium from organic matter decomposition to nitrite and nitrate available to phytoplankton; Thaumarchaeota may be the most abundant archaea on Earth, reaching 10⁴–10⁵ cells per milliliter in the mesopelagic zone; their discovery as nitrifiers overturned decades of textbook knowledge attributing marine nitrification exclusively to bacteria; their tiny genome (1.6 Mb in Candidatus Nitrosopumilus maritimus) is the smallest known for any free-living archaeon capable of autotrophic growth, enabling energy-efficient chemolithotrophy in nutrient-limited ocean interiors.

source.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

text: The continental shelf represents only 8% of ocean area but supports 90% of global marine fish production, because shallow depths allow sunlight penetration to the seafloor, nutrient-rich river and upwelling inputs stimulate phytoplankton blooms, and structural habitat (seagrass, kelp, coral, rocky reef) provides nursery and shelter for commercially important species; the world's richest continental shelf fisheries—Grand Banks, Bering Sea, North Sea, Yellow Sea—now show cumulative human impacts from fishing, pollution, eutrophication, and hypoxia that reduce their productivity relative to historical baselines, with ecosystem-based management required to maintain productivity.

Deep-sea sponges (Hexactinellida and Demospongiae) are extraordinary filterers, capable of processing up to 50,000 liters of water per kilogram of sponge per day, extracting picoplankton and dissolved organic matter from otherwise oligotrophic deep water; sponge grounds on the Norwegian shelf and in the deep North Atlantic function as 'pumps' cycling nutrients between the benthic and pelagic zones, and host diverse associated communities of brittle stars, polychaetes, and crustaceans; the sponge loop—uptake of dissolved organic matter followed by release of particulate detritus through choanocyte cell shedding—represents a previously unknown pathway supporting diverse sponge-ground food webs.

Trophic efficiency—the percentage of energy transferred from one trophic level to the next—averages approximately 10% in marine food webs, meaning 10,000 kg of phytoplankton produces about 1,000 kg of zooplankton, 100 kg of forage fish, and ultimately 10 kg of tuna or 1 kg of apex predator; this rule explains why it is far more efficient to harvest low on the food chain (filter feeders, small pelagic fish) than high (tuna, swordfish), and why feeding humans on fish meal requires 5–10 kg of wild fish per kg of farmed salmon; the efficiency varies with temperature, species, and ecosystem productivity and is reduced by climate warming that shifts communities toward smaller cells and longer food chains.

source.name: Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics

text: The Indonesian Throughflow (ITF) transports approximately 15 Sverdrup of warm, relatively fresh Pacific water through the narrow passages of the Indonesian archipelago into the Indian Ocean, representing a critical link in the global thermohaline circulation; the ITF moderates Indian Ocean temperatures and salinity, influences monsoon rainfall across South Asia and East Africa, and modulates ENSO dynamics by ventilating the Western Pacific warm pool; paleoclimate evidence from sediment cores shows that changes in ITF strength during glacial cycles corresponded with major reorganizations of the Indian Ocean monsoon system and regional sea level differences between the Pacific and Indian Oceans.

Cumulative human impacts on the global ocean, mapped from 2008 to 2019, show that 59% of ocean area and 99% of the ocean's territorial waters experience medium-high to very high cumulative impact from shipping, climate change, fishing, pollution, and coastal development simultaneously; no ocean area on Earth is entirely free from human influence; the most heavily impacted regions are the North Sea, Yellow Sea, Mediterranean, and Caribbean, while the least impacted remain parts of the Southern Ocean and central Pacific; areas with high biodiversity (tropical reefs, seamounts) overlap extensively with high impact zones, making conservation urgent.

The Arctic sea route—including the Northern Sea Route along Russia's coast and the Northwest Passage through Canada's Arctic Archipelago—has seen a 50-fold increase in shipping traffic since 2010 as sea ice retreats; while Arctic shipping cuts 7,000–12,000 km from Europe-Asia voyages, it introduces ballast water-transported invasive species to ecologically naive polar communities, creates underwater noise in biologically sensitive habitats, and risks oil spills in ice-laden waters where cleanup is nearly impossible; the IMO Polar Code (2017) established mandatory safety and environmental standards for polar ships, but enforcement remains challenging given the remoteness and sparse monitoring.

The Benguela ecosystem's 'anchovy-sardine-round herring' alternation, Pacific 'sardine-anchovy' regimes, and North Sea 'gadoid outburst' of the 1960s exemplify how fish populations can shift abruptly between alternative states driven by multi-decadal climate variability and fishing pressure interactions; regime shifts can be difficult to detect in real time and may be irreversible on management-relevant timescales; the Pacific sardine (Sardinops sagax) collapse in the 1940s—made famous by John Steinbeck's Cannery Row—was long attributed solely to overfishing but is now understood as a combination of fishing and cold PDO regime shift, with recovery requiring both reduced fishing and favorable climate.

The planet's ocean basins—Pacific (165 million km², 50% of world ocean), Atlantic (82 million km²), Indian (73 million km²), Arctic (14 million km²), and Southern (21 million km²)—differ fundamentally in age, shape, and circulation; the Pacific, oldest and deepest (average 4,280 m), is rimmed by the Ring of Fire producing 90% of Earth's earthquakes and 80% of its volcanoes; the Atlantic is younger (opened 100-200 Ma), widening at 2.5 cm/year; the Indian Ocean hosts the most intense monsoon system; the Southern Ocean, defined by the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, is unique in being bounded by currents rather than land, enabling unobstructed circumpolar flow.

The concept of the 'shifting baseline syndrome,' first articulated for fisheries by Daniel Pauly in 1995, applies forcefully to ocean science: each generation of marine biologists perceives the degraded state of the ocean at the beginning of their career as the natural or historical baseline, systematically underestimating the extent of change; historical ecology using catch records, naturalists' accounts, and archaeological midden analysis reveals that pristine baselines included bluefin tuna 100x more abundant than today, cod schools visible from ships, grey whales in the Mediterranean, and monk seals on European beaches, changes invisible in the living memory of current scientists.

The mangrove-seagrass-coral reef connectivity system, best studied in the Caribbean, demonstrates how different coastal habitat types function as an integrated ecosystem: juvenile fish (snapper, grunt, barracuda) recruit to seagrass beds nursery areas, migrate to mangroves for refuge at night, and as adults migrate to coral reefs to spawn; reefs and seagrass beds are 30–100 times more productive when connected to mangroves than when isolated, and coral reefs adjacent to intact mangroves showed 4–6 times higher fish biomass; coastal development fragments these connections, contributing to reef fish decline even when the reefs themselves appear intact.

Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) are classified as marine mammals and depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting ringed seals (Pusa hispida), their primary prey; declining Arctic sea ice is reducing foraging success, causing population-wide declines in body condition and reproductive success, with the southern Beaufort Sea subpopulation declining 40% in 10 years; polar bear populations in areas experiencing earlier sea ice breakup spend more months fasting on land, burning fat reserves accumulated over shorter hunting seasons; projections under high emissions scenarios suggest severe impacts on most polar bear subpopulations by 2100, with southern populations facing local extinction.

The Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua) collapse on the Grand Banks off Newfoundland—from 250,000 tonnes annual catch in the 1960s to near-zero by 1992, triggering the largest fishery closure in history affecting 40,000 people—is the definitive cautionary tale of industrial overfishing; despite a moratorium now exceeding 30 years, cod populations have not recovered due to changed ecosystem conditions, predation by increased seal populations, and potential dietary and structural shifts in the ecosystem that may represent a regime shift with multiple stable states; the collapse demonstrated that CPUE (catch per unit effort) can remain stable while overall abundance collapses due to fishers concentrating effort on remaining aggregations.

Kelp forests—dominated by giant kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera) in the eastern Pacific, Ecklonia in Australia and South Africa, and Laminaria in the North Atlantic—support up to 800 associated species and provide coastal storm protection worth an estimated $1.1 billion annually to California alone; giant kelp grows up to 60 cm per day, creates a three-dimensional habitat structure spanning from the seafloor to the ocean surface, and sequesters carbon at rates comparable to tropical forests per unit area; sea urchin population explosions caused by the loss of sunflower sea stars (killed 99% by sea star wasting disease since 2013) have created extensive urchin barrens in Northern California, devastating the abalone and rockfish fisheries.

The abalone (genus Haliotis) is among the most valued shellfish globally, with live red abalone worth USD 60–100/kg in California and black abalone historically supporting Indigenous food systems along North American Pacific coasts; wild populations have collapsed to 1–5% of historical levels from overfishing and withering syndrome (a rickettsial bacterial disease weakening digestive glands); CRISPR-based genetic tools are being applied to understand disease resistance in abalone populations, and hatchery supplementation programs have restored some populations in protected areas; global aquaculture now produces 70,000+ tonnes of abalone annually, primarily in South Africa, China, and Australia.

source.name: Reviews in Fisheries Science and Aquaculture

text: Cephalopod arms and suckers contain distributed neurons with local processing capabilities analogous to spinal cord ganglia in vertebrates, so that each arm can perform semi-autonomous searching behavior while the central brain sets higher-level goals; this decentralized nervous system with two-thirds of neurons in the arms enables octopus to solve complex manipulation tasks (opening childproof bottles, navigating mazes) while allowing independent exploratory arm movements the brain does not directly coordinate; cuttlefish show REM-like sleep states with rapid eye movements and body pattern flickering, suggesting they may experience dream-like states analogous to those of vertebrates.

The 2023 anomalous North Atlantic sea surface temperature event—reaching 0.5–1.5°C above the previous record for the region—generated significant scientific debate about drivers; proposed explanations include reduced stratospheric aerosol loading after the 2022 Hunga Tonga volcanic eruption (which increased atmospheric water vapor rather than aerosols), the 2020 IMO shipping sulfur emission regulations (reducing reflective sulfate aerosols from shipping routes), and natural AMOC variability; the event contributed to record hurricane activity and anomalous European weather, highlighting the need for improved attribution science for regional ocean warming episodes.

Coral bleaching is caused by thermal stress breaking down the molecular machinery of photosynthesis in zooxanthellae symbionts, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) that the coral expels along with the zooxanthellae; without algal symbionts providing up to 90% of its energy via photosynthesis, the coral turns white and starves; bleaching is triggered by temperatures approximately 1°C above the average monthly maximum for as little as 4 weeks; following bleaching, corals can recover if temperatures decrease within 2–4 weeks, but mortality approaches 100% after 8–12 weeks at bleaching temperatures; the frequency of bleaching events has increased from once per 25–30 years in the 1980s to once per 3–5 years currently.

The halocline—a sharp salinity gradient in the water column—is particularly critical in the Arctic Ocean, where a 30–50 m thick, cold, low-salinity layer derived from river runoff, sea ice meltwater, and Pacific Water inflow insulates sea ice from the warmer, saltier Atlantic Water below; this Arctic halocline reduces heat flux from the warm Atlantic layer to the sea ice by 10–20 W/m²; freshening of the Arctic Ocean from increased precipitation, river runoff, and Greenland melt is strengthening the halocline, potentially insulating sea ice from Atlantic warming while also affecting deep water formation and thermohaline circulation in the Nordic Seas.

Dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) produced by marine phytoplankton is cleaved to dimethyl sulfide (DMS) by bacteria, producing 28.1 Tg sulfur/year that volatilizes to the atmosphere where it oxidizes to sulfate aerosols acting as cloud condensation nuclei; the CLAW hypothesis (Charlson, Lovelock, Andreae, Warren, 1987) proposed that this created a negative feedback loop: warming → more algae → more DMS → more clouds → more solar reflection → cooling; subsequent research has shown the feedback exists but is insufficient to counteract greenhouse warming; DMS remains the primary biogenic climate-relevant gas from the ocean and a focus of geoengineering proposals.

The global ocean contains approximately 37,000 Gt of carbon in dissolved inorganic form (bicarbonate and carbonate ions), compared to only 800 Gt in the atmosphere; this 46:1 ratio means the ocean is the primary carbon reservoir exchanging with the atmosphere on human timescales, and slight changes in ocean carbon chemistry drive major changes in atmospheric CO₂; during glacial periods, lower ocean temperatures, increased iron-fertilized biological production, and expanded deep-water formation contributed to atmospheric CO₂ levels approximately 80–100 ppm lower than interglacials, demonstrating the ocean's fundamental role in glacial-interglacial CO₂ cycles.

The Sea of Japan/East Sea provides a 'miniature ocean' model for studying climate change impacts at accelerated rates due to its regional warming (3 times faster than global average surface oceans), isolated water masses, and excellent Japanese and Korean monitoring records spanning 100+ years; dissolved oxygen has decreased 20% since the 1970s, jellyfish blooms have increased 10-fold, and cold-water species such as snow crab and Alaskan pollock have shifted northward into Russian waters; its semi-enclosed nature and strong seasonal stratification makes it particularly sensitive to warming compared to adjacent open-ocean regions, providing an early warning system for Pacific Ocean changes.

The North Atlantic's 'biological production engine' is powered by winter deep mixing that replenishes nutrients in the photic zone, followed by spring stratification and the onset of the North Atlantic Spring Bloom; satellite ocean color sensors have tracked this bloom's timing, intensity, and geographic extent since 1979, revealing that it has advanced 8 days per decade in some regions as earlier stratification driven by warming reduces winter mixing depth; primary production in the high-latitude North Atlantic is projected to decline 20–40% by 2100 under high emissions due to increased stratification limiting nutrient supply to phytoplankton.

Intertidal zones serve as natural laboratories for ecology due to their visible zonation—barnacles, mussels, algae, and periwinkles distributed in distinct bands by tidal exposure, wave action, and predation—and their accessibility for experimental manipulation; Robert Paine's classic experiments on Tatoosh Island removing Pisaster sea stars demonstrated that removing the keystone predator caused mussels to eliminate 15 other species, reducing intertidal diversity by half; Connell's work on barnacle zonation on Scottish shores established foundational principles of competitive exclusion and physical stress determining community assembly still cited in introductory ecology texts.

text: Riftia pachyptila tube worms at hydrothermal vents grow at 60–80 cm per year—the fastest growth rate of any known marine invertebrate—to reach 2 m length within 2 years of vent colonization; they completely lack a mouth, digestive tract, and anus, obtaining all nutrition from 10¹⁰ sulfur-oxidizing endosymbiotic bacteria per gram of specialized trophosome tissue that occupies most of the worm's body cavity; the worm's remarkable hemoglobin carries both oxygen and hydrogen sulfide simultaneously to the bacteria without either toxifying the other—a biochemical feat achieved by spatially separated binding sites that makes Riftia hemoglobin the most complex known in biology.

Seascape genetics—combining population genetics with oceanographic connectivity models—reveals how ocean currents, thermal barriers, and seabed topography shape gene flow among marine populations; genetic breaks in species previously thought to have homogeneous, open-ocean populations have been discovered at major current boundaries (the Almeria-Oran Front in the Mediterranean, the Cape Point in South Africa), and fine-scale local adaptation has been detected in cod, oysters, and seagrasses at scales of 10–100 km; these findings challenge fisheries management units based on phenotypic or geographic boundaries, as genetically distinct populations may require separate quotas and conservation measures.

The phosphorus cycle, unlike nitrogen, has no significant gaseous phase, making it entirely dependent on weathering of crustal minerals and recycling from sediments; phosphorus is the ultimate limiting nutrient on geological timescales because nitrogen fixation can compensate for nitrogen deficiency but nothing can replace phosphorus lost to burial; ocean phosphorus inventory turns over approximately every 20,000–100,000 years, and its variations in the geological past drove massive changes in marine productivity and ocean oxygenation, including the Neoproterozoic snowball Earth glaciation recovery and the Devonian mass extinction—demonstrating that phosphorus cycling is a master control on Earth's biosphere.

text: The ocean's role in human culture, food security, and climate regulation makes it arguably the most important ecosystem on Earth: covering 71% of the planet's surface, absorbing 93% of excess heat, 26–34% of CO₂ emissions, and supplying 3.3 billion people with their primary protein source; every second breath of oxygen originates from marine phytoplankton; ocean fisheries and aquaculture directly employ 600 million people; marine natural products have yielded over 30 approved pharmaceuticals and hundreds in clinical trials; and the cultural, spiritual, and recreational values of the ocean are irreplaceable for the majority of humanity that lives within 100 km of the coast—making its conservation a prerequisite for sustainable human civilization.

Microbiome research on coral reefs has revealed that the coral holobiont—the coral animal, its algal symbionts, bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses together—functions as a superorganism whose collective metabolism determines reef resilience; different microbiome compositions characterize healthy versus bleached versus diseased corals, and transplanting microbiome communities between corals can transmit disease states; the coral 'probiotics' field is testing whether inoculating stressed corals with bacteria known to suppress ROS, fix nitrogen, or reduce pathogen colonization can improve thermal tolerance; early mesocosm experiments show 40% improvements in survival under experimental bleaching conditions.

The Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) has been confirmed as the world's longest-lived vertebrate through radiocarbon dating of eye lens nuclei that retain isotopic signatures fixed during embryogenesis; the largest specimen analyzed was estimated at 392 ± 120 years, placing its birth in the late 17th century; Greenland sharks grow only 1 cm per year and do not reach sexual maturity until approximately 150 years of age, making their populations extraordinarily vulnerable to any fishing mortality—even low bycatch levels may exceed sustainable harvest; their longevity has attracted interest for studying negligible senescence and the molecular biology of extreme aging.

Biogenic silica cycling by diatoms—which extract dissolved silicic acid from seawater to build their frustule cell walls—controls silicon availability in the surface ocean and influences carbon export efficiency; in the Southern Ocean, the silica trap traps silicon in sinking diatom frustules before it can reach warmer northern waters, limiting diatom productivity throughout the world ocean; as Southern Ocean warming and ice reduction alter diatom community structure, this silica limitation may propagate to reduce diatom production and efficient carbon export across multiple ocean basins, creating large-scale effects on the biological pump from a relatively localized physical change.

Oyster aquaculture provides valuable ecosystem services alongside food production: a single adult oyster filters 190 liters of water per day, removing suspended sediments, excess nutrients, and pathogens; restored oyster reefs along the Virginia coast improve water clarity by 30% within 5 years, enabling seagrass recovery; oyster shells create three-dimensional reef structure providing habitat for juvenile fish and invertebrates; the global aquaculture industry produces approximately 5.4 million tonnes of oysters annually—primarily in China (80%)—primarily using longline culture that does not contact the seafloor and causes minimal habitat disturbance, unlike many other forms of aquaculture.

The deep ocean carbon reservoir of approximately 37,000 Gt DIC (dissolved inorganic carbon) exchanges with the atmosphere on a 200–1,000 year timescale as deep waters upwell to the surface; this 'geological carbon pump' ensures that even if all surface ocean CO₂ uptake stopped, equilibration with the deep ocean would eventually pull atmospheric CO₂ back down over centuries; however, the 500–1,000 year residence time of CO₂ in the deep ocean means that anthropogenic CO₂ emitted today will continue warming the atmosphere long after emissions cease, committing future generations to decades of sea level rise, ocean acidification, and marine ecosystem disruption regardless of near-term mitigation.

Pacific Island nations' exclusive economic zones contain the world's largest tropical tuna fisheries, and their 200 nm EEZ boundaries drawn by UNCLOS provide formal resource rights worth billions annually despite controlling no major fishing vessels of their own; the Parties to the Nauru Agreement (PNA) Vessel Day Scheme auction daily fishing access rights, generating USD 500–800 million annually for eight small island nations and demonstrating that UNCLOS-derived resource sovereignty can be effectively converted to economic value by developing nations through collective management; this model is being studied as a template for other regions seeking to benefit from marine genetic resources under the BBNJ Treaty.

Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) undertake an anadromous life cycle—spawning in cold freshwater rivers, migrating to the North Atlantic for 1–4 years of ocean feeding, and returning to their natal river guided by olfactory memory of dissolved compounds—and serve as biological links transporting marine-derived nutrients (nitrogen-15 isotope tracers) to freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems; wild Atlantic salmon populations have declined 80% in 40 years, driven by dam obstruction of migration routes, habitat degradation, aquaculture sea lice transmission, climate-driven changes in freshwater growth conditions, and shifts in North Atlantic prey availability; their recovery is a whole-watershed and ocean-scale conservation challenge.

The photic zone—the sunlit upper ocean where photosynthesis occurs—extends to approximately 200 m depth in the clearest open-ocean waters but only 10–30 m in turbid coastal and productive regions; it contains only 0.5% of ocean volume but generates 50 Gt C/year of primary production supporting virtually all marine life above the deep sea; satellite ocean color sensors measure chlorophyll concentrations as a proxy for phytoplankton biomass, revealing seasonal cycles, El Niño impacts, and long-term trends in primary production; global primary production may have declined 6–10% since the 1980s as warming-driven stratification reduces nutrient supply, though regional trends diverge.

Marine genetic resources—DNA, proteins, and biochemical compounds from marine organisms—are an emerging frontier with pharmaceutical, industrial, and biotechnological applications; deep-sea and vent organisms have yielded thermostable enzymes, antibiotic compounds, and potential anticancer molecules; the BBNJ Treaty's provisions for equitable benefit sharing from genetic resources found in international waters, inspired by the Nagoya Protocol, represent a major innovation in ocean governance; 73% of patents on marine genetic resources are currently held by ten companies and research institutions in Germany, the USA, and Japan, raising equity concerns that the treaty aims to address through access and benefit-sharing mechanisms.

The ocean's future under different climate scenarios diverges dramatically: at 1.5°C, the Arctic remains seasonally ice-covered until at least 2100, coral reefs decline 70–90%, and sea level rise is limited to 30–60 cm by 2100; at 2°C, the Arctic loses summer sea ice regularly, 99% of coral reefs are severely bleached annually, AMOC may approach tipping points, and sea level could reach 60–110 cm; at 3–4°C (current trajectory with existing policies), multiple ocean tipping points—AMOC collapse, West Antarctic Ice Sheet destabilization, marine ecosystem regime shifts—could be crossed within this century, committing Earth to thousands of years of fundamentally altered ocean circulation, chemistry, and biodiversity that no human generation will see resolved.

Environmental DNA (eDNA) monitoring—detecting species presence by sequencing DNA shed into the water from skin, feces, mucus, and gametes—is transforming marine biodiversity assessment: a single 1-liter water sample filtered through a membrane can yield detectable eDNA from hundreds of species simultaneously via metabarcoding; eDNA surveys of Port Phillip Bay (Australia) detected 260 fish species, 40% more than traditional trawl surveys; eDNA has confirmed presence of the critically endangered Maui dolphin (population ~63) in habitats not surveyed for decades, and detected spawning aggregations of rare fish by identifying egg DNA; challenges include DNA degradation rates, transport by currents, and reference database completeness for matching sequences to species.
